Empirical Research Plan  
“Public Transit Strikes and Road‐Traffic Congestion in Los Angeles, 2002–2003”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Main approach: Difference-in-Differences (DID) embedded in an event-study panel.

Why DID?  
• Strikes created sharp, plausibly exogenous ON/OFF variation in subway service.  
• Traffic can be observed on the same road segment before, during, and after each strike period.  
• Cross-sectional heterogeneity in expected exposure (distance to a subway station) supplies a credible control group.  
• High-frequency (daily) panel allows flexible event-study checks of the parallel-trends assumption.

Secondary robustness: 2-stage least squares (2SLS) treating “strike day” as an instrument for actual daily train frequency; reported only as a robustness check.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Unit of analysis: road-segment-day (i, t).

Treatment variable
  Ti  = 1{ road-segment centroid ≤1 mile of any subway station }  
  (Alternative intensity measure: 1/Distance or #stations within 1 mile.)

Strike indicator
  St  = 1 on days in which labor action cut scheduled subway service ≥80 %.  
  Strikes: Jan 14–18 2003 slowdown; Aug 1–6 2003 stoppage; Oct 14–24 2003 full MTA strike.

DID interaction (the “shock”):
  Di,t = Ti × St

Control group
  Road segments >2½ miles from every subway station (not bordering freeways that parallel the subway corridor).  
  These roads face the same city-wide shocks (weather, gasoline price) but are much less likely to be used by regular subway riders.

Timing
  Pre-period: 60 days before first strike day of each event.  
  Post-period: 60 days after service resumes.  
  Event-time dummies k ∈ [-60, +60] used for the dynamic specification.

No running variable / cutoff is required (not an RDD design).

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of a strike, treated and control road segments would have evolved similarly.  
   Plausibility: Both sets are in the same metropolitan area and subject to the same overall demand shocks. We will test with pre-event coefficients.

A2. Exogeneity of strikes: Timing, duration, and intensity of the labor actions were not tied to day-to-day traffic conditions on specific roads.  
   Plausibility: Strikes are driven by contract negotiations; daily traffic speeds do not influence union decisions.

A3. No spillovers to control roads: Extra cars diverted from subway riders do not significantly change congestion on far-away control segments.  
   Plausibility: 2½-mile buffer and exclusion of freeway segments reduces risk but cannot eliminate it entirely; we will conduct distance-gradient robustness.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): Congestion on a segment is unaffected by whether nearby segments are labeled treated or control, conditional on observables.  
   Plausibility: Congestion externalities decay quickly with distance; we additionally cluster by corridor to allow correlated shocks.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Baseline differences in road characteristics  
   • Mitigation: Road-segment fixed effects absorb time-invariant attributes; control for lane count, speed limit interacted with time.

T2. Other contemporaneous shocks (e.g., gasoline price spikes, large sports events)  
   • Mitigation: Date fixed effects; weather, gas price, and major-event controls; event-study window narrow enough to limit confounders.

T3. Spatial spillovers lowering control purity  
   • Mitigation: Vary distance cutoffs (1 mi vs 0.5 mi vs 2 mi) and report gradient estimates; show that farthest-away segments are insensitive to strikes.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# -------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# -------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# -------------------------------
traffic <- fread("la_traffic_2002_2003.csv")        # speeds & volumes
transit <- fread("subway_service_2002_2003.csv")    # #trains/hour etc.
stations <- fread("subway_stations.csv")            # lat/long

# -------------------------------
# 2. Merge & Variable Construction
# -------------------------------
# a) distance to nearest station
coords <- as.matrix(stations[,.(lat, lon)])
traffic_coords <- as.matrix(traffic[,.(lat, lon)])
traffic[, dist_station := geosphere::distHaversine(traffic_coords, coords[ knn::knn(coords, traffic_coords, k = 1)$nn.idx , ]) / 1609.34 ] # miles

# b) treatment dummy
traffic[, treat := (dist_station <= 1)]

# c) strike days list
strike_dates <- as.Date(c("2003-01-14":"2003-01-18",
                          "2003-08-01":"2003-08-06",
                          "2003-10-14":"2003-10-24"))
traffic[, strike := as.Date(date) %in% strike_dates]

# d) DID interaction
traffic[, did := treat * strike]

# e) outcome variables
traffic[, ln_speed := log(avg_speed)]
traffic[, ln_volume := log(traffic_volume+1)]

# -------------------------------
# 3. Baseline DID Regression
# -------------------------------
did_speed <- feols(ln_speed ~ treat*strike | segment_id + date,
                   data = traffic, cluster = ~segment_id)
summary(did_speed)

# -------------------------------
# 4. Event-Study Specification
# -------------------------------
# create event time (k) for each strike episode
traffic[, k := as.numeric(date - fifelse(strike, date, NA), units="days"), by = segment_id]
traffic <- traffic[ abs(k) <= 60 ]      # window ±60 days
event_mod <- feols(ln_speed ~ sunab(k, treat) | segment_id + date,
                   data = traffic, cluster = ~segment_id)
iplot(event_mod)                        # parallel-trend graph

# -------------------------------
# 5. Robustness Check: Distance Gradient
# -------------------------------
traffic[, dist_bin := cut(dist_station,
                          breaks = c(0,0.5,1,2,5,Inf),
                          labels = c("0-0.5","0.5-1","1-2","2-5","5+"))]

grad_mod <- feols(ln_speed ~ i(dist_bin, strike, ref="5+") |
                     segment_id + date,
                  data = traffic, cluster = ~segment_id)
etable(grad_mod)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Economic prediction: With subway unavailable, commuters substitute toward cars, raising congestion.  
Sign of main coefficient on did (treat × strike): negative for speed (speeds fall), positive for volume.  
Magnitude (prior): 5 – 10 % lower average speed on treated roads during strikes, i.e., β̂ ≈ ‑0.05 to ‑0.10 in logs.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Parallel pre-trends visible in event-study graph .......... 1  
C2: No anticipatory effects before strike ..................... 1  
C3: Treatment unrelated to time-varying confounders ........... 0.5 (city-wide shocks possible)  
C4: No spillovers to control units ............................ 0.5  
C5: Correct functional form / standard errors ................. 1  

Total (out of 5) = 4.0

Overall, the design leverages abrupt, externally imposed service outages and detailed spatial traffic data to deliver credible causal estimates of how public transit availability mitigates urban road congestion.
